headline: Princeton Grads Deploy First-of-Its-Kind Microplastic Filter in Atlantic City
meta_description: A nature-inspired filtration device removes microplastics from wastewater at scale, protecting the Atlantic Ocean and human health.
summary_short: Princeton alumni have built the world's first large-scale microplastic filter for wastewater, now operating in Atlantic City with 98% removal efficiency.
body:
Two Princeton architecture graduates have designed and deployed what may be the world's first commercially viable system to filter microplastics from wastewater at scale. The device, created by Nathanial Banks and Yidian Liu through their startup PolyGone Technologies, mimics hydrophobic plants found in nature—drawing water away while attracting microplastic particles that can then be collected and recycled. The system is now operating in Atlantic City, a city of 40,000, as part of a two-year pilot program run by the Atlantic County Utilities Authority. Laboratory tests showed the prototype could remove 98 percent of microplastic particles from wastewater, and the pilot will test whether this efficiency can be maintained at commercial scale.

Microplastics enter wastewater through everyday sources: washing machines, heavy rains, and littering. Most treatment facilities across the country aren't equipped to handle them, focusing instead on human sewage, solids, and heavy metals. Yet microplastics have been found everywhere researchers look—from the ocean floor to mountaintops, and inside human organs. Matt DeNafo, president of the ACUA, emphasized the stakes: "If we're not removing the plastic that's in our wastewater, we're putting it back into the environment. It's getting into the fish that we're eating, even the water that we're bathing."

What's remarkable about Banks and Liu's approach is its simplicity and scalability. Unlike energy-intensive solutions, their device uses very little material and minimal power while treating a challenging contaminant at size. The pair are already exploring smaller versions for residential use, with another commercial-scale implant now operating in California. No federal regulation currently mandates microplastic removal, yet the ACUA chose not to wait—a choice that may inspire other utilities to take similar action before the problem becomes even more entrenched.
quick_facts: Princeton graduates designed first world-scale microplastic wastewater filter
Device removes 98% of microplastics in laboratory tests
Now operating in Atlantic City through two-year pilot program
Technology mimics nature-based hydrophobic plant design
